title: IBM Launches Directed Execution Model and Executor Primitive to Give Researchers Client-Side Control Over QEC Workflows - Quantum Computing Report
gist: IBM Quantum launched a directed execution model and Executor primitive in qiskit-ibm-runtime v0.50.0, moving error mitigation from a server-side black box to client-side, composable control. Early users report a 3.4-fold PEC overhead cut and up to a 2.8-fold logical error reduction per round on distance-5 surface codes on Nighthawk.

themes.theme: Shift of error mitigation from server to client

insights.claim: IBM Quantum introduced a directed execution model, powered by a new Executor primitive in qiskit-ibm-runtime v0.50.0, that moves error mitigation logic from a server-side black box to the client side.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: IBM is opening up its runtime stack to give researchers control, a move toward transparency that may deepen developer lock-in to Qiskit tooling.
insights.locator: IBM Quantum has introduced a new

insights.claim: Rather than generating and shipping thousands of randomized circuits over the network, developers define execution blueprints locally with annotations and template parameter tensors, and the Executor expands them in the near-time environment of the IBM Quantum Compute Service.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Cutting client-to-server circuit transfer overhead is a practical scaling fix for workloads needing large families of circuit variants.

insights.claim: The Executor handles shot loops, tensor parameter sweeping and broadcasting across 5,000+ circuit randomizations.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete scale for the randomization workloads the new primitive is built for.

insights.claim: The existing high-level Sampler and Estimator primitives now run on top of the Executor as a client-side wrapper, making the v0.50.0 upgrade non-disruptive for standard users while letting them inspect and customize resilience options such as TREX in local simulation before committing to QPUs.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Rebuilding the high-level APIs on the new primitive means the whole user base migrates with little friction, accelerating adoption.

insights.claim: The architecture is a layered stack: Qiskit SDK v2.0+ boxes and annotations (Twirl, InjectNoise, ChangeBasis), the open-source samplomatic library, the Executor, NoiseLearnerV3, and the open-source qiskit-mitigation package.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: IBM is productizing mitigation and QEC workflows as modular, open components, a platform play in the software layer of quantum.
insights.locator: Core Components of the Directed Execution Architecture

insights.claim: qiskit-mitigation supplies modular routines for Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Zero-Noise Extrapolation and Twirled Readout Error Extinction, while NoiseLearnerV3 provides client-side sparse Pauli-Lindblad and TREX noise learning for unique circuit layers.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Noise characterization moving client-side lets third parties build custom mitigation, widening the ecosystem around IBM hardware.

insights.claim: The client-side transparency is pitched as a unified platform spanning quantum error mitigation and full quantum error correction.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Positions one software stack as the bridge between near-term mitigation and fault-tolerant QEC, a continuity story for IBM's roadmap.
insights.quote: The client-side transparency enabled by directed execution provides a unified platform spanning quantum error mitigation and full quantum error correction.

insights.claim: Researchers using the framework combined Probabilistic Error Cancellation with Shaded Lightcones to cut PEC sampling overhead 3.4-fold.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Sampling overhead is the main cost of PEC, so a 3.4x reduction extends the range of problems mitigation can reach on current hardware.
insights.locator: Researchers are already using the framework

insights.claim: Researchers ran distance-5 surface codes on IBM Quantum Nighthawk processors using the framework, achieving up to a 2.8-fold reduction in logical error rates per round.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Evidence of below-threshold-style QEC progress on IBM hardware, though the article gives no baseline or detail.
insights.locator: Researchers are already using the framework

insights.claim: The article says this infrastructure directly supports recent milestone demonstrations, including IBM's trusted quantum advantage results with ecosystem partners.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The link to advantage claims is asserted without evidence, so treat it as IBM-aligned framing.
